answer.rationale: memory_c2 is the load-bearing memory this cycle: it is the only record that would justify moving primary supply to the low-cost vendor, and it is exactly the record whose framing is thinnest. It reports unit cost, onboarding speed and invoicing accuracy — it says nothing about on-time delivery rate, quality escapes, or whether that vendor ever carried volume at a line running with no buffer. It is also dated 'last year' and consolidated on day 38, so it may describe a different volume tier and a different vendor capacity position than today. Pulling the original record tells me whether the cost win came with delivery performance data or whether the delivery dimension simply was never measured. With the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, a primary-vendor switch executed in 14 days concentrates all the risk on the one axis the objective forbids increasing. So my current intent is to negotiate terms with the incumbent, using the low-cost quote as the benchmark instrument — this is the pattern memory_c4 records as having actually recovered margin, and memory_c6 indicates the incumbent has volume-pricing headroom that a multi-year structure can unlock, which is a second lever toward the 18% mandate without touching supply continuity. memory_c1 supports that the incumbent relationship absorbs no migration cost. I am treating this as a guarded step rather than a settled answer: negotiation is reversible and keeps the switch and second-source options alive for the next review, whereas a switch now is not reversible inside this cycle. Explicit residual uncertainty: (a) negotiation may not close the full 18% gap, in which case the switch or a hybrid dual-source becomes the next-cycle candidate; (b) if the archive shows memory_c2's vendor did carry comparable volume with clean delivery, the risk case against switching weakens materially and I would revisit. Downstream value risk: an 18% spend cut pursued purely on unit price can be paid for later in quality escapes, expedite freight, and line-stoppage cost that never appears in the component-spend line finance is measuring — cost is being optimized on a narrower metric than total cost of ownership, and I am flagging that the mandate's success measure and the stated objective are not the same measure.
